Welcome to _The Rust Programming Language_, an introductory book about Rust. Rust helps you write faster, more reliable software. In programming language design, high-level ergonomics and low-level control are often at odds, and Rust challenges that conflict. By balancing technical power with a good developer experience, it lets you control low-level details (such as memory usage) without the hassle traditionally associated with that control.

## Who Rust is for

Rust is a good fit for many people, for a variety of reasons. Here are a few of the most important groups.

### Teams of developers

Rust is proving to be a productive tool for large teams of developers with varying levels of systems programming knowledge to work together. In most other languages, low-level code is prone to subtle bugs that can only be caught through extensive testing and careful code review by experienced developers. In Rust, the compiler acts as a gatekeeper: it refuses to compile code with these elusive bugs, concurrency bugs included. Working alongside the compiler, the team can spend its time on the program's logic instead of chasing down bugs.

Rust also brings contemporary developer tools to the systems programming world:

- Cargo, the included dependency manager and build tool, makes adding, compiling, and managing dependencies painless and consistent across the Rust ecosystem.
- The `rustfmt` formatting tool ensures a consistent coding style across developers.
- The Rust Language Server powers integrated development environment (IDE) integration for code completion and inline error messages.

The cayote is a living, breathing allegory of Want. He is *always* hungry.

He is always poor, out of luck and friendless. The meanest creatures despise him, and even the fleas would desert him for a velocipede. He is so spiritless and cowardly that even while his exposed teeth are pretending a threat, the rest of his face is apologizing for it. And he is so *homely*!—so scrawny, and ribby, and coarse-haired, and pitiful. When he sees you he lifts his lip and lets a flash of his teeth out, and then turns a little out of the course he was pursuing, depresses his head a bit, and strikes a long, soft-footed trot through the sage-brush, glancing over his shoulder at you, from time to time, till he is about out of easy pistol range, and then he stops and takes a deliberate survey of you; he will trot fifty yards and stop again—another fifty and stop again; and finally the gray of his gliding body blends with the gray of the sage-brush, and he disappears. All this is when you make no demonstration against him; but if you do, he develops a livelier interest in his journey, and instantly electrifies his heels and puts such a deal of real estate between himself and your weapon, that by the time you have raised the hammer you see that you need a minie rifle, and by the time you have got him in line you need a rifled cannon, and by the time you have “drawn a bead” on him you see well enough that nothing but an unusually long-winded streak of lightning could reach him where he is now. But if you start a swift-footed dog after him, you will enjoy it ever so much—especially if it is a dog that has a good opinion of himself, and has been brought up to think he knows something about speed.

# Rate limiting

Rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable. This page covers how the Gateway handles it.

## How it works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Clients should treat this as a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

These settings let you balance protecting your services against giving your users a smooth experience.

Noise-cancelling headphones can seem like magic, but they rely on an elegant principle called destructive interference. They don't only block sound. They fight it with more sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less reaches your ears.

The effect works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work from home, or just value quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose headphones with more information behind the decision.

final: Whether remote work raises employee productivity is still hotly debated in organizational research. Okafor et al. (2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). The benefits appear to depend heavily on task type, though. Moreau, Tanaka, and Ellis (2021) caution that "the effects of remote work are neither uniformly positive nor uniformly negative" (p. 46). Researchers need to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. Hearing it hurt.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

For a second Nora couldn't answer. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands weren't steady. She hadn't touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun came through the fog. He wasn't really gone, Nora thought. He was in every gear and spring, and in the patience he had taught her. Grief was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still had his name over the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, as he had.

The Harbor County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on Tuesday to approve a $48 million expansion of the Route 9 bus line. The plan adds 11 new stops and extends service hours to midnight.

"This is about giving people a real alternative to driving," said Supervisor Lena Kowalczyk, who sponsored the measure. "For a lot of families in the east county, the bus is the only way to get to work."

Supervisor Mark Deaver, who cast the lone dissenting vote, argued that the plan relies too heavily on state matching funds. "If Sacramento pulls back, we're left holding the bill," he said.

According to a 2024 county survey, 38% of east county households do not own a car. Ridership on Route 9 has grown 22% since 2022, reaching roughly 6,400 weekday boardings.

Construction is expected to begin in March, with the first new stops opening by fall 2026. The expansion is meant to make transportation more equitable, sustainable, and accessible for all residents.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well-suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

In distributed systems, rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable. This page covers how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. The client should treat this as a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Together, these settings let you protect your services without making things worse for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones can seem like magic, but they work through destructive interference: they fight sound with sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup constantly sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less noise reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work from home, or just value peace and quiet, knowing this can help you choose a better pair.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora came back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air inside smelled of old brass. The bell above the door gave its usual chime. She stood there a moment before she let the door close behind her.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he'd been repairing when the stroke took him, the back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

Nora looked at the floor. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

When he'd gone, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch started to tick.

Outside, the fog was thinning and the sun came through. He wasn't really gone, she thought. He was in every gear and spring, and in the patience he'd taught her. Grief was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still had his name over the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

The Harbor County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on Tuesday to approve a $48 million expansion of the Route 9 bus line, adding 11 new stops and extending service hours to midnight.

"This is about giving people a real alternative to driving," said Supervisor Lena Kowalczyk, who sponsored the measure. "For a lot of families in the east county, the bus is the only way to get to work."

Supervisor Mark Deaver, who cast the lone dissenting vote, argued that the plan relies too heavily on state matching funds. "If Sacramento pulls back, we're left holding the bill," he said.

According to a 2024 county survey, 38% of east county households do not own a car. Ridership on Route 9 has grown 22% since 2022, to roughly 6,400 weekday boardings.

Construction is expected to begin in March, with the first new stops opening by fall 2026.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, not well suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable. Here is how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait, so the client knows to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Together, these settings let you protect your services while keeping the experience smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones work by destructive interference: they cancel sound with more sound instead of only blocking it.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the ambient noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, which sharply reduces what reaches your ears.

The technique works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, such as the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, like a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work remotely, or just value peace and quiet, knowing this can help you choose a pair.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street. The shop smelled of old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime, and it hurt to hear it.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

Nora was quiet a moment. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

Outside, the sun broke through the fog. Her father wasn't gone, she thought. He was in the gears and springs, in the patience he had taught her, in the steady rhythm of time. Grief was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

The Harbor County Board of Supervisors voted 4-1 on Tuesday to approve a $48 million expansion of the Route 9 bus line. It adds 11 new stops and extends service hours to midnight.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and are not well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting keeps your APIs stable and reliable by capping how much traffic each client can send. This page covers how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. The response tells the client to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Together, these settings let you balance protecting your services against keeping things smooth for your users.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway with flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

Nora could barely get the words out. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't held a pair of tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun was breaking through the fog outside. Her father wasn't really gone, Nora thought. He was in every gear and spring, and in the patience he had taught her. Grief was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later the shop still had his name over the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, just as he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and aren’t well suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, is available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting keeps your APIs stable and reliable. This page covers how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. The response is a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

These settings let you balance protecting your services against keeping things smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones might seem like magic, but they rely on destructive interference. They block some sound, and they also fight the rest with sound of their own.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the ambient noise around you. This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner, generally below about 1,000 Hz. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like peace and quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a better pair.

A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that is the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, greatly reducing what reaches your ears.

Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work from home, or just like peace and quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a better pair.
<<<END>>>

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora returned to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had, and her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, a single tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

Nora swallowed. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands trembled. She had not touched tweezers in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. He wasn't gone, she thought, not entirely. He was in every gear and spring, and in the patience he had taught her. Grief was just love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later his name was still above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and they aren’t well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, is available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable. Here is how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait. Clients should treat this as a signal to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

These settings let you balance protecting your services against keeping things smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones might seem like magic, but they rely on destructive interference. Instead of just blocking sound, they fight it with more sound.

Here's how it works. Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip generates a sound wave that is the mirror image of that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and much less reaches your ears.

The technique works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel, which is why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

Whether you fly a lot, work from home, or just like quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a pair.

Whether you fly a lot, work from home, or just like quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a pair.
<<<END>>>

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora came back to her father's shop, a thin fog hung over Delancey Street, and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell above the door gave its familiar chime. Her chest went tight.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging together. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw resting beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

Nora's throat was thick when she answered. "I should have come back sooner."

"He understood. He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. He wasn't really gone, she thought. He was in every gear and spring, in the patience he'd taught her, in the steady rhythm of time. Grief was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still bore his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, as he had.

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there's some task you'd like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you'd like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you're a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you're writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you've written a program that could use an extension language, and you don't want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and aren't well suited to GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use, is available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python allows you to split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.

## Getting Started

**lintwise** is a fast, lightweight, configurable linter for YAML files. Whether you're managing Kubernetes manifests or CI pipelines, it helps you catch errors before they reach production.

### Installation

lintwise requires Python 3.10 or later. Install it with pip:

```bash
pip install lintwise
```

### Usage

Point lintwise at a file or directory:

```bash
lintwise check ./config
```

By default, lintwise checks indentation, duplicate keys, and trailing whitespace. To customize the rules, create a `.lintwise.toml` file in your project root. lintwise exits with code 1 if it finds any errors, so it's easy to add to a CI workflow.

The evidence is strong. According to the California Air Resources Board, a typical commercial gas blower emits more smog-forming pollution in an hour than a car does over roughly 1,100 miles of driving. Workers who operate them for hours a day face serious risks to their hearing. And the high-pitched whine carries for blocks, disrupting remote workers, sleeping infants, and anyone trying to enjoy a quiet afternoon.

Some landscapers worry about the cost of switching to battery equipment, and that concern deserves to be taken seriously. Cities can ease the transition by phasing in bans gradually and offering rebates. The case for a ban is clear, and the result would be quieter, cleaner, healthier communities for everyone.

Marcus found his brother on the back porch, looking out at the dark orchard. It smelled of rain and overripe apples, and the crickets were loud in the tall grass.

"So you're really selling," Marcus said.

Daniel didn't turn around. "The bank isn't giving us a choice. Dad left us more debt than trees."

Marcus's throat went tight. "This orchard was his whole life. We grew up here. It's who we are, Danny."

"I know." Daniel's voice cracked. "But holding on to it won't pay the mortgage. Maybe letting go is the only way to honor what he built."

Marcus sat down beside him on the worn steps. Neither of them said anything for a long time. Somewhere in the orchard, an apple dropped.

"Okay," Marcus finally said. "But I'm keeping his pruning shears."

Daniel laughed, a small, broken sound, and Marcus thought they would be all right.

Welcome to _The Rust Programming Language_, an introductory book about Rust. The Rust programming language helps you write faster, more reliable software. High-level ergonomics and low-level control are often at odds in programming language design; Rust challenges that conflict. By balancing powerful technical capacity with a great developer experience, Rust lets you control low-level details (such as memory usage) without the hassle traditionally associated with that control.

## Who Rust Is For

Rust suits many people for many reasons. Here are a few of the most important groups.

### Teams of Developers

Rust is proving to be a productive tool for collaboration among large teams of developers with varying levels of systems programming knowledge. Low-level code is prone to various subtle bugs, which in most other languages can only be caught through extensive testing and careful code review by experienced developers. In Rust, the compiler acts as a gatekeeper: it refuses to compile code with these elusive bugs, concurrency bugs included. Working alongside the compiler, the team can spend its time on the program’s logic rather than chasing down bugs.

Rust also brings contemporary developer tools to the systems programming world:

- Cargo, the included dependency manager and build tool, makes adding, compiling, and managing dependencies painless and consistent across the Rust ecosystem.
- The `rustfmt` formatting tool ensures a consistent coding style across developers.
- The Rust Language Server powers integrated development environment (IDE) integration for code completion and inline error messages.

With these and other tools in the Rust ecosystem, developers can be productive while writing systems-level code.

The cayote is a living, breathing allegory of Want. He is *always* hungry.

He is always poor, out of luck and friendless. The meanest creatures despise him, and even the fleas would desert him for a velocipede. He is so spiritless and cowardly that even while his exposed teeth are pretending a threat, the rest of his face is apologizing for it. And he is so *homely!*—so scrawny, and ribby, and coarse-haired, and pitiful. When he sees you he lifts his lip and lets a flash of his teeth out, and then turns a little out of the course he was pursuing, depresses his head a bit, and strikes a long, soft-footed trot through the sage-brush, glancing over his shoulder at you, from time to time, till he is about out of easy pistol range, and then he stops and takes a deliberate survey of you; he will trot fifty yards and stop again—another fifty and stop again; and finally the gray of his gliding body blends with the gray of the sage-brush, and he disappears. All this is when you make no demonstration against him; but if you do, he develops a livelier interest in his journey, and instantly electrifies his heels and puts such a deal of real estate between himself and your weapon, that by the time you have raised the hammer you see that you need a minie rifle, and by the time you have got him in line you need a rifled cannon, and by the time you have "drawn a bead" on him you see well enough that nothing but an unusually long-winded streak of lightning could reach him where he is now. But if you start a swift-footed dog after him, you will enjoy it ever so much—especially if it is a dog that has a good opinion of himself, and has been brought up to think he knows something about speed.

# Rate Limiting

Rate limiting helps keep your APIs stable and reliable. Here is how the Gateway handles it.

## How It Works

The Gateway uses a fixed-window algorithm. Each client, identified by its API key, gets a budget of requests per window. When a client exceeds its budget, the Gateway responds with HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait, so the client knows to back off.

## Configuration

Add a `rate_limit` block to your `gateway.yaml`:

```yaml
rate_limit:
  max_requests: 100
  window_seconds: 60
  burst: 20
```

| Setting | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `max_requests` | 100 | Requests allowed per window |
| `window_seconds` | 60 | Length of the window in seconds |
| `burst` | 0 | Extra requests allowed above the limit |

`burst` defaults to 0, so bursts are disabled unless you set it explicitly. For more details, see https://docs.example.com/gateway/rate-limits.

Together, these settings let you balance protecting your services against keeping things smooth for your users.

Noise-cancelling headphones might seem like magic, but they rely on destructive interference. They fight sound with sound.

Tiny microphones on the outside of each ear cup continuously sample the noise around you. A dedicated chip then generates a sound wave that mirrors that noise, shifted 180 degrees out of phase. When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and far less reaches your ears.

This works best on low-frequency, constant sounds, generally below about 1,000 Hz, like the hum of an airplane engine or the drone of an air conditioner. Sudden, high-pitched noises, such as a baby crying or a door slamming, are much harder to cancel. That's why most headphones also rely on the passive seal of the ear cushions.

If you fly a lot, work remotely, or just value peace and quiet, knowing how this works can help you choose a pair.

(2018) ran a randomized experiment with 249 call-center employees and found a 13% increase in performance among those assigned to work from home. A later meta-analysis of 46 studies (Lindqvist & Haddad, 2020) reported small but positive effects on supervisor-rated performance (d = 0.12). Researchers need to look more closely at the boundary conditions that shape remote work outcomes.

The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog lay over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner." Her voice came out thick.

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. He wasn't really gone, she thought. He was in every gear and spring, in the patience he had taught her, in the steady rhythm of time itself. Grief was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still had his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.

- "Her chest tightened" and "throat felt thick" did the same job, so I kept the chest and made the second one her voice coming out thick.
- Beyond that I trimmed adjectives and the stock "familiar chime" and "patient unison".
- Two things are left for you to decide, since cutting either changes the ending. The "Years later" coda could go, so the story ends on the watch ticking. The last two lines of the realization paragraph could also go.

<<<FINAL>>>
The Clockmaker's Daughter

The morning Nora went back to her father's shop, a thin fog lay over Delancey Street and the air smelled of rain and old brass. The bell over the door chimed the way it always had. Her chest tightened.

Nothing had changed. Dozens of clocks lined the walls, their pendulums swinging in unison. On the workbench lay the pocket watch he had been repairing when the stroke took him, its back still open, one tiny screw beside it.

Mr. Alvarez from the bakery next door appeared in the doorway, flour on his sleeves. "He talked about you every day," he said. "He was so proud of you."

"I should have come back sooner." Her voice came out thick.

"He understood," Mr. Alvarez said. "He always said you had your own clocks to wind."

After he left, Nora sat at the bench and picked up the watch. Her hands shook. She hadn't touched a tweezer in eleven years, but her fingers remembered. She seated the screw, closed the case, and wound the crown. The watch began to tick.

The sun broke through the fog outside. He wasn't really gone, she thought. He was in every gear and spring, in the patience he had taught her, in the steady rhythm of time itself. Grief was love with nowhere to go, until you gave it somewhere.

Years later, the shop still had his name above the door, and Nora still wound every clock each morning, the way he had.
<<<END>>>

If you do much work on computers, eventually you find that there’s some task you’d like to automate. For example, you may wish to perform a search-and-replace over a large number of text files, or rename and rearrange a bunch of photo files in a complicated way. Perhaps you’d like to write a small custom database, or a specialized GUI application, or a simple game.

If you’re a professional software developer, you may have to work with several C/C++/Java libraries but find the usual write/compile/test/re-compile cycle is too slow. Perhaps you’re writing a test suite for such a library and find writing the testing code a tedious task. Or maybe you’ve written a program that could use an extension language, and you don’t want to design and implement a whole new language for your application.

Python is just the language for you.

You could write a Unix shell script or Windows batch files for some of these tasks, but shell scripts are best at moving around files and changing text data, and not well suited for GUI applications or games. You could write a C/C++/Java program, but it can take a lot of development time to get even a first-draft program. Python is simpler to use and available on Windows, macOS, and Unix operating systems, and it will help you get the job done more quickly.

Python lets you split your program into modules that can be reused in other Python programs. It comes with a large collection of standard modules that you can use as the basis of your programs — or as examples to start learning to program in Python. Some of these modules provide things like file I/O, system calls, sockets, and even interfaces to graphical user interface toolkits like Tk.

He always reminds me of my poor Uncle Podger. You never saw such a commotion up and down a house, in all your life, as when my Uncle Podger undertook to do a job. A picture would have come home from the frame-maker's, and be standing in the dining-room, waiting to be put up; and Aunt Podger would ask what was to be done with it, and Uncle Podger would say:

"Oh, you leave that to *me*. Don't you, any of you, worry yourselves about that. *I'll* do all that."

And then he would take off his coat, and begin. He would send the girl out for sixpen'orth of nails, and then one of the boys after her to tell her what size to get; and, from that, he would gradually work down, and start the whole house.

"Now you go and get me my hammer, Will," he would shout; "and you bring me the rule, Tom; and I shall want the step-ladder, and I had better have a kitchen-chair, too; and, Jim! you run round to Mr. Goggles, and tell him, 'Pa's kind regards, and hopes his leg's better; and will he lend him his spirit-level?' And don't you go, Maria, because I shall want somebody to hold me the light; and when the girl comes back, she must go out again for a bit of picture-cord; and Tom!—where's Tom?—Tom, you come here; I shall want you to hand me up the picture."

And then he would lift up the picture, and drop it, and it would come out of the frame, and he would try to save the glass, and cut himself; and then he would spring round the room, looking for his handkerchief. He could not find his handkerchief, because it was in the pocket of the coat he had taken off, and he did not know where he had put the coat, and all the house had to leave off looking for his tools, and start looking for his coat; while he would dance round and hinder them.
